topStories.headline: Planning Commission Clears 536 Mission for a 46-Story Tower — But Cuts the Office Allocation in Half
topStories.dek: Commissioners approved the SoMa skyscraper project on September 10 but rejected the developer's bid for the full Prop M office allowance, keeping a mixed-use option alive.
topStories.body:
The San Francisco Planning Commission voted on September 10 to grant downtown project authorization for a proposed 46-story tower at 536 Mission Street in SoMa, where Golden Gate University's campus currently stands. The site sold for $31.6 million earlier that week, clearing the way for the hearing. Developers Lincoln Property Company and McCourt Partners — working with architect Skidmore, Owings & Merrill — have pursued two variants: a purely commercial tower rising 752 feet with nearly 1.35 million square feet of office space, and a mixed-use alternative topping out around 697 feet that would include approximately 385 residential units alongside office floors.

The commission approved authorization for both design variants and made shadow findings, but drew the line on office square footage. Brandon Wong, executive vice president of Lincoln Property Company, asked commissioners to allocate the full 813,214 square feet of Prop M office capacity available to the project — enough to make the all-office tower financially viable. That motion failed 2–4. A subsequent motion adopted the planning staff's recommendation of 555,390 square feet, a figure staff said represented a prudent allotment given remaining citywide Prop M availability.

The practical effect is significant. At 555,000 square feet of office allocation, the commercial-only variant becomes harder to finance at the scale Lincoln prefers, nudging the project toward the mixed-use option that city planners explicitly favored. Planning Department spokesman Patrick Hannon said the department's preference was the residential variant because it 'contributes to downtown revitalization while also producing much needed housing.' Construction is expected to take roughly four years from groundbreaking once the project moves forward through remaining entitlement steps.

The outcome lands amid SoMa's broader split personality. The SF Standard's September 3 survey of the neighborhood described Fifth Street as a dividing line: east of it, large office leases are being signed and Moscone Center conference schedules are full; west of it, storefronts remain dark and the neighborhood still bears deep pandemic-era scars. A 46-story tower at the eastern edge of SoMa, if built, would become one of the five or six tallest buildings in the Bay Area.
topStories.sourceName: Citizen Portal / SF Planning Commission Record

topStories.headline: District 10 Race Enters the Home Stretch: Where the Candidates Stand Seven Weeks Out
topStories.dek: With 59 days until the November 3 election, Mission Local this week published the latest installment of its weekly candidate Q&A series, keeping the open-seat race in focus for Potrero Hill and Dogpatch voters.
topStories.body:
The race to succeed termed-out District 10 Supervisor Shamann Walton — who covers Potrero Hill, Dogpatch, Bayview-Hunters Point, Visitacion Valley, and surrounding neighborhoods — is now in its final two months, and the field remains unusually large. Ten candidates qualified for the November 3 ballot, and Mission Local published its most recent 'Meet the Candidates' installment on September 17, this week asking each candidate to respond in 100 words or fewer to questions about the city's new homelessness nonprofit contracting overhaul.

Three candidates have attracted the most institutional attention. Theo Ellington, a public policy director who previously ran for the seat in 2018, was the first in the race to qualify for public matching funds through the SF Ethics Commission — receiving an initial $60,000 grant — and holds endorsements from former Mayor Willie Brown, Supervisor Connie Chan, and Supervisor Myrna Melgar, among others. Dion-Jay 'DJ' Brookter, a community organizer and nonprofit director, and attorney J.R. Eppler round out the most visible tier of candidates. Eppler is listed as a participant in the Potrero Hill R&B Festival in October, reflecting his strong local-neighborhood roots.

The most recent multi-candidate debate before Potrero Hill voters was held September 1 at the Potrero Hill Neighborhood House, hosted by the Potrero Hill Democratic Club, the Potrero Boosters Neighborhood Association, and moderated by Mission Local's Joe Eskenazi. The debate was largely cordial but touched on the district's longstanding grievances: inequitable city budget allocations, housing, environmental justice at the former Hunters Point Naval Shipyard, and the pace of development at Pier 70. All three candidates at that forum acknowledged the district's history as under-resourced. 'We make sure that the southeast side of San Francisco gets the same energy, investment, and resources as the rest of the city,' Ellington said at the event, per the Gazetteer SF's account. Voting begins in mid-October; the general election is November 3.

topStories.headline: Mission Bay Elementary Opens Its Doors — The Neighborhood's First Public School in 28 Years
topStories.dek: The $95 million campus at 1415 Owens Street welcomed its first students on August 17, completing a journey that began with the 1998 Mission Bay Redevelopment Plan.
topStories.body:
Mission Bay Elementary School held its ribbon-cutting on August 6, with Mayor Daniel Lurie and SFUSD Superintendent Dr. Maria Su in attendance, and welcomed its first pre-kindergarten, transitional kindergarten, and kindergarten students on August 17. The school, at 1415 Owens Street near the UCSF Medical Center, is the first new public school SFUSD has opened in more than 20 years and the first public elementary school ever built to serve Mission Bay's rapidly growing resident population.

The four-story, 81,800-square-foot building cost $95.4 million, constructed by McCarthy Building Companies and funded primarily by Proposition A, the school bond voters approved in 2016. SFUSD plans to phase in additional grade levels through the 2031–32 school year, eventually serving up to 550 students from pre-K through fifth grade. The school also includes a science and technology center for high school students, with apprenticeship and research programs.

The opening fulfills a commitment embedded in Mission Bay's 1998 redevelopment plan, when the neighborhood was still a patchwork of abandoned rail yards. The Mission Bay neighborhood has nearly doubled in population over the past 15 years, and competition for seats in the Daniel Webster Attendance Area — which covers SoMa, Mission Bay, Potrero Hill, and Dogpatch — had become fierce. Mission Bay Elementary now shares that attendance area with Daniel Webster, giving families in the eastern neighborhoods a genuine neighborhood school option for the first time.

moreNews.headline: Treasure Island's First Condo Building Now Open, Completing Phase One
moreNews.body: 490 Avenue of the Palms, a six-story, 148-unit building at Treasure Island, opened for leasing in July 2026 as the first condominium-configured residential complex on the island, completing Stage 1 of the Treasure Island master plan. The project was co-developed by the Treasure Island Development Group — a partnership of Lennar Corporation, Stockbridge Capital Group, and Wilson Meany — and is managed as a rental by Sentral. Two earlier communities on the island, Isle House and Hawkins, are each more than 90 percent leased, and the island now has eight completed parks. The broader master plan targets 8,000 homes, 300 acres of open space, and roughly 27 percent affordable housing across Treasure Island and Yerba Buena Island.

moreNews.headline: Mission Bay Transportation Advisory Committee Meets This Month
moreNews.body: The Mission Bay Transportation Improvement Fund Advisory Committee has a regular September 2026 meeting scheduled through the SFMTA. The committee oversees the use of transportation funds generated by Mission Bay development fees to fund transit and street improvements in and around the neighborhood. Residents with concerns about traffic, transit access, or pedestrian safety in Mission Bay can attend or submit public comment; details are posted on the SFMTA website.
